text.hook:
You write new every week.
But can you say what it does, in which order, and what happens when it fails?

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Storage is not an object
2. The pairing rules
3. When the constructor throws
4. Wire buffers and what malloc really costs
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Storage vs object, pairing rules, failure, and what malloc really costs.

slides.title: Storage is not an object

cards.label: Storage
cards.text: Raw bytes with an address. Can exist with no object in it.

cards.label: Object
cards.text: Typed. Lifetime starts when construction completes, ends when its destructor starts.

cards.label: Same storage, new object
cards.text: Destroy, then construct again at the same address: a **new** object. Keep the pointer placement new returns.

slides.takeaway: Pools, `std::launder` and wire buffers all follow from keeping storage and lifetime apart.

slides.title: Release it the way you got it
slides.takeaway: Any mismatch is UB, even when it "works". `delete nullptr` is a no-op: never write `if (p) delete p;`.

slides.title: `new Order(-1)`, step by step
steps: no leak, and no destructor: the object never existed

slides.title: Your `T::operator new` is skipped by

cards.label: Arrays
cards.text: `new T[n]` uses `T::operator new[]` only if you declare it.

cards.label: Global scope
cards.text: `::new T` explicitly selects the global allocation function.

slides.takeaway: If the class allocator exists for correctness (shared memory, a special heap), each bypass is a bug.

slides.title: Casting a receive buffer to `Header*` breaks
items: Object model: no `Header` was ever created there
Strict aliasing: only `char`, `unsigned char`, `std::byte` may alias anything
Alignment: the offset may be odd, and misaligned access is UB
Layout: padding and byte order must match the wire

slides.lead: Most small `new` calls are a lock-free tcache pop. Rare paths take a lock, a syscall and page faults: that ruins p99.9.

items.myth: "Same address, same type: it's the same object."
items.truth: A new lifetime is a new object. Old pointers stay valid only under the transparent-replacement rules.

items.myth: "Every `new` takes a lock and makes a system call."
items.truth: The common path is a user-space tcache pop (glibc). The slow paths are rare but unpredictable.
`new T` default-initializes: an `int` or trivial members are indeterminate. `new T()` and `new T{}` zero them.

items.myth: "`new` of a few GB throws `bad_alloc` if RAM is short."
items.truth: Linux overcommits: it usually succeeds. Pages arrive on first touch; the OOM killer acts later.

items.myth: "RSS keeps growing, so it is a leak."
items.truth: Retention, fragmentation, kept capacity and unbounded queues grow RSS even when every block is freed.

slides.hero:
`new` = allocate + construct.
`delete` = destroy + free.

Pair them exactly.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Three orders allocated with new[]. One delete.
At worst that leaks two objects, right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: It compiles. For some types it even seems to work, which is why it survives code review.

slides.title:
What happens at run time?
(x86-64, GCC + glibc)

slides.verdict_sub: GCC + glibc: "munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer". Undefined behaviour.
bullets: `new Order[3]` stores the count in an 8-byte cookie before the array (Itanium ABI).
It returns a pointer **past** that cookie.
Plain `delete` runs one destructor, then frees the shifted address: not the start of any allocation.
`new int[3]` has no cookie and may "work". Still UB: ASan reports `alloc-dealloc-mismatch`.

slides.title: Match the form, or own nothing

columns.label: delete[]
std::vector

text.hook:
64 TiB requested with plain new, then with nothrow.
The code even checks for nullptr. What prints?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Two forms of new, two different failure contracts. Mixing them up leaves dead error handling in real code.

slides.title: What prints? (Linux x86-64)

slides.verdict_sub: Linux x86-64, default overcommit: 64 TiB is more than the kernel will reserve, so both fail at once
bullets: So the `if (p == nullptr)` branch is dead code.
Under ASan it aborts instead, unless `allocator_may_return_null=1`.

slides.title: Each form needs its own check
slides.takeaway: Linux overcommit: 8 GiB on a 16 GB box usually *succeeds*. Failure comes later, as an OOM kill when pages are touched.

text.hook:
"new T and operator new are the same thing."
This program disagrees.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Get this one right and placement new, pools and allocation counters all make sense.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: `operator new` = allocate only. `new T` = allocate + construct
bullets: `operator new(std::size_t)` returns raw bytes, like `malloc`. No constructor.
`new T` calls `operator new`, then constructs a `T` in that storage.
`delete p` mirrors it: destructor first, then `operator delete(p)`.
You can overload or replace `operator new`. You cannot change the new-expression.
slides.wrong: "`operator new` is just the name of the `new` keyword"

slides.title: Raw bytes need placement new
slides.code:
void* raw = operator new(sizeof(T));
T* t2 = new (raw) T;   // prints "ctor "
t2->~T();              // end the object
operator delete(raw);  // free the bytes
bullets: Placement new = the new-expression with a non-allocating `operator new(size_t, void*)`.
slides.takeaway: Pools, allocation counters and custom heaps hook in at `operator new`. Construction always stays with the new-expression.

text.hook:
An Order built with placement new in a stack buffer.
Four engineers, four cleanup lines. Three of them are bugs.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Pool slots, inline storage and shared memory all use this exact pattern.

slides.title: Which cleanup is correct?

slides.verdict_sub: Placement new allocates nothing: it constructs in storage you own
bullets: Whoever owns the storage releases it: here, the stack frame.
Afterwards the storage can hold another object.
The storage must be big enough, aligned for `Order`, and free of live objects.
slides.wrong: "`delete p` frees the buffer so it can't be reused"
slides.cta: Why not A, B or C ➜

items: A: `delete` runs the destructor, then frees a stack address. ASan: "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed".
B: `free` gets a stack address too (same ASan error), and the destructor never runs.
C: the bytes go away, but `~Order()` never runs. The 40-char string's heap buffer leaks (LeakSanitizer: 41 bytes).
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "In generic code write `::new (static_cast<void*>(addr)) T(...)` or `std::construct_at`, so class-specific placement overloads are not picked up."
